system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-09-12 09:01:00 to 2179-09-16 13:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of severe Crohn’s disease, status post multiple abdominal surgeries including colectomy and ileostomy takedown, was admitted with worsening abdominal pain and decreased stool frequency following a Tysabri infusion. Imaging revealed findings concerning for a partial small bowel obstruction, likely due to a combination of inflammatory stricture and adhesions. He was managed conservatively with bowel rest, NG tube decompression, IV fluids, and pain control. His renal function improved from acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration. Anxiety was managed with quetiapine after lorazepam was discontinued due to confusion. MR enterography confirmed stable active inflammation in the distal ileum without abscess or stricture. Pain resolved, diet was advanced, and he was discharged home on Percocet for breakthrough pain, continued prednisone and Tysabri, with follow-up arranged.
problems: Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

microbiology.comments: Feces negative for C. difficile toxin A & B by EIA.            (Reference Range-Negative).

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I’ve been reviewing your case. You came in last night with abdominal pain and frequent diarrhea—can you tell me more about how it started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started around midnight. I had this sharp pain in my lower left side, coming in waves. Then I went to the bathroom eight times between 2 and 3 a.m.—all watery, no blood in the stool, but I saw blood on the toilet paper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you said this feels similar to past Crohn’s flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Not like my kidney stone pain—it doesn’t go to my back or groin. This is more like the cramping I’ve had before when my Crohn’s acts up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. You also mentioned you’ve been off prednisone for about a week. That might be a trigger. We’re going to run some tests to rule out infection and check your inflammation levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on Tysabri for a few months now. Should I still get my next dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were due for it today, but we’re holding off until we confirm this is a flare and not an infection. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work came back. White count is normal, no sign of infection. CRP is slightly elevated at 4.5, which suggests inflammation. Blood cultures are negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably Crohn’s again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks that way. Your kidney function is a bit off—creatinine is 1.3, up from your baseline of 1.1. That’s likely from dehydration due to the diarrhea. We’re giving you IV fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray of your abdomen is back. Good news—no sign of a blockage or obstruction. Bowel gas pattern is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about another surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll avoid that if we can. The plan is to treat this as a Crohn’s flare. We’re starting you on IV steroids—solumedrol every eight hours—to reduce the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to go back on prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once we transition from IV. We’ll start you on 40 mg daily. We also want to do a flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to confirm the flare and take biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Biopsies? Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s important to make sure it’s active inflammation and not an infection like CMV. Your CMV serologies came back negative, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scope went well. We saw ulceration and inflammation in the rectosigmoid and ileum—classic Crohn’s pattern. We took biopsies from both areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it’s definitely Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The preliminary read shows chronic active ileitis with ulceration—very consistent with Crohn’s. No granulomas or dysplasia. We’ll also start you on hydrocortisone enemas nightly to target the rectal inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using loperamide, but it’s not helping much with the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it on board for symptom control, but the steroids and enemas should reduce the inflammation causing the diarrhea. We’ll hold off on antibiotics since stool C. diff was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some tenderness in the lower left side, but not the waves of pain I had. I slept through the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your creatinine is down to 1.1—kidneys are recovering with fluids. We’ll keep the IVs going a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re advancing your diet to clear liquids today. If that goes well, we’ll move to low-residue solids tomorrow. Avoid anything too fibrous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look stable. Hemoglobin is 12.5, slightly down but not concerning. Platelets and white count are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but also from the flare and being NPO. As you start eating and the inflammation calms, your energy should improve. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is minimal, you’re tolerating food, and your labs are improving. We’re switching you from IV solumedrol to oral prednisone—same 40 mg dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on this long-term again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting at 40 mg, but you’ll taper it down with your GI doctor. The goal is to get you off, but we need to control this flare first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about Tysabri? I’m worried about stopping it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held this dose, but GI thinks it’s safe to restart as an outpatient. You’ll follow up with them in a week to decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed this rash on my left leg—it’s itchy and I keep scratching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that—some excoriations and dried blood. It looks like a chronic eczematous rash. We’ll give you bacitracin ointment to prevent infection and suggest you avoid scratching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. It’s been bothering me for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. Your pain is much better, you’re eating well, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take prednisone 40 mg daily, tapering as directed by GI. Continue the hydrocortisone enema every night for 18 more days. For pain, you’ll have extended-release morphine twice daily for three days, and oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—omeprazole twice daily, loperamide four times daily, and your monthly B12 injection. Apply bacitracin to the rash twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call to schedule within the week. They’ll decide on continuing Tysabri and your steroid taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as needed. But if you have fever, worsening pain, or heavy bleeding, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid any foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-residue for now—white bread, rice, bananas. Avoid raw veggies, nuts, and seeds until your GI appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll keep a food log.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent idea. That’ll help your GI team adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enemas—I use them at bedtime, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every night. They help reduce rectal inflammation. You should notice less bleeding and urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. That was scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re on the mend. Just follow the plan, and you’ll keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of severe Crohn’s disease, status post multiple abdominal surgeries including colectomy and ileostomy takedown, was admitted with acute abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. The presentation was consistent with a Crohn’s flare, likely triggered by recent discontinuation of prednisone. Infection was ruled out with negative blood, stool, and urine cultures. Imaging showed no obstruction. A flexible sigmoidoscopy confirmed active inflammation in the rectosigmoid and ileum, with biopsy findings of chronic active ileitis. He was treated with IV solumedrol, transitioned to oral prednisone, and started on hydrocortisone enemas. Acute kidney injury due to dehydration resolved with IV fluids. His pain and diarrhea improved, and he was discharged on a prednisone taper, enemas, and short-term pain medication with follow-up arranged with gastroenterology.
